scope: Twelve exact original short AS-mock Physics/Chemistry recall cards; no A2, no Maths, no new duplicated cards
method: Preserve original questions and saved IDs. Match exact original front/back, add two reviewed correct variants and two known wrong variants, test real production evaluator and reject known contradictions before fuzzy marking.
limitation: Targeted marker quality improvement only; not AQA atomic-coverage certification. Unseen acceptable paraphrases or handwritten answers still require review.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: Why can intense light below the threshold frequency still emit no photoelectrons?
rows.originalBack: Each photon still has too little energy to overcome the work function. Greater intensity gives more photons, not higher-energy photons.
accept: Below threshold, every photon still has insufficient energy for emission; more intense light only brings more photons.
Even with lots of photons, hf is less than the work function so no electrons escape.
reject: High intensity makes each photon energetic enough to release electrons despite below-threshold frequency.
Sufficient intensity compensates for insufficient frequency by adding the energies of many photons.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What is excitation of an atom?
rows.originalBack: A bound electron moves to a higher allowed energy level, staying in the atom.
accept: An electron rises to a higher allowed bound energy level without escaping the atom.
Excitation is a bound electron absorbing energy to occupy a higher energy state.
reject: Excitation removes an electron from the atom entirely, leaving a positive ion.
Excitation means a bound electron drops to a lower level and releases a photon.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalBack: An electron is removed from an atom, leaving a positive ion.
accept: Ionisation removes an electron from an atom to leave a positive ion.
An electron completely escapes from the atom, producing a cation.
reject: Ionisation only promotes an electron to another bound level in the same atom.
Ionisation makes a positive ion by adding an electron to the atom.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalBack: Energy gained by an electron moved through 1 V; 1 eV = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ J.
accept: One electronvolt is the energy transferred to a charge equal to e through one volt: 1.60 × 10^-19 J.
1 eV = 1.60 x 10^-19 joule, the energy change for one elementary charge across 1 V.
reject: One electronvolt is the energy of one electron moving through 1 ampere.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What observation shows wave behaviour of electrons?
rows.originalBack: Their diffraction into rings or interference patterns through a crystal.
accept: A diffraction pattern formed when electrons pass through a thin crystal shows wave behaviour.
Electrons produce interference/diffraction rings in a crystal, revealing a wave nature.
reject: Electrons never diffract through crystals; they only move as classical particles.
Electron diffraction is evidence that electrons have no wave properties.

rows.subject: Physics
rows.originalFront: What observation shows the particle nature of light?
rows.originalBack: The photoelectric effect: light transfers energy in photons.
accept: Photoelectric emission shows light arrives in packets of energy called photons.
The photoelectric effect demonstrates photon-by-photon energy transfer.
reject: The double-slit interference pattern by itself proves light cannot behave as a wave.
Photoelectric emission shows that light transfers energy continuously and never in photons.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What does a very large successive-IE jump identify?
rows.originalBack: Removal has reached an inner shell; the number removed before it equals outer-shell electrons.
accept: A sharp ionisation-energy jump shows removal reached an inner shell; the number removed before it equals the outer-shell electrons.
After the outer electrons have gone, an inner-shell electron needs much more energy; the count before this jump gives the outer electrons.
reject: A very large jump means the next electron is further from the nucleus in an outer shell.
It means shielding suddenly increases greatly for the next electron, making it easier to remove.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is Hund's rule when filling degenerate orbitals?
rows.originalBack: Electrons occupy equal-energy orbitals singly before pairing.
accept: In degenerate orbitals, electrons fill each orbital singly before they pair.
Hund's rule says one electron enters each equal-energy orbital before electrons are paired.
reject: Hund's rule says fill one p orbital with two electrons before any other p orbital receives one.
Pair every electron immediately in the first degenerate orbital before occupying the next.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the electron configuration of Cr³⁺?
rows.originalBack: [Ar]3d³. Remove the 4s electron first, then two 3d electrons.
accept: Cr3+ has the ground-state electron configuration [Ar]3d3.
The configuration of chromium(III) is [Ar] 3d³ after losing the 4s electron and two 3d electrons.
reject: Cr³⁺ has [Ar]3d5.
Cr³⁺ has [Ar]3d³4s².

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the electron configuration of Cu²⁺?
rows.originalBack: [Ar]3d⁹. Remove one 4s electron and then one 3d electron.
accept: Cu2+ has the electron configuration [Ar]3d9.
Copper(II) is [Ar] 3d⁹ after losing 4s and one 3d electron.
reject: Cu²⁺ has [Ar]3d10.
Cu²⁺ has [Ar]3d⁹4s².

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: What is the electron configuration of Cu⁺?
accept: Cu+ has the configuration [Ar]3d10.
Copper(I) is [Ar] 3d¹⁰, with its 4s electron removed.
reject: Cu⁺ has [Ar]3d9.
Cu⁺ has [Ar]3d⁹4s¹.

rows.subject: Chemistry
rows.originalFront: Which two different causes explain the Period 3 first-IE dips?
rows.originalBack: Mg→Al: higher-energy 3p versus 3s. P→S: extra repulsion from paired 3p electrons.
accept: Mg to Al: 3p electron is at higher energy than 3s. P to S: paired 3p electrons repel.
Al loses an electron from a higher-energy 3p subshell than Mg; S has extra repulsion between paired 3p electrons unlike P.
reject: Mg to Al: aluminium loses a lower-energy 3s electron. P to S: there is no pairing effect.
Both drops happen because the electrons move into a completely new principal shell.
